svg.aria-label: Structure of a replication fork with helicase, leading strand continuous synthesis, lagging strand Okazaki fragments, primase and ligase
svg.text: The replication fork
Every DNA polymerase synthesises only 5' to 3' and cannot start without a primer. These two limits force the two strands to be copied differently.
parental duplex (not yet unwound)
heli-
case
fork moves
LEADING STRAND
one primer, then continuous synthesis
in the same direction as the fork
LAGGING STRAND
Okazaki fragments, each with its own primer,
made away from the fork
bacteria 1000-2000 nt; eukaryotes 100-200 nt
gap sealed by DNA ligase
Proteins at the fork
helicase: unwinds using ATP (DnaB in bacteria, MCM in eukaryotes)
single-strand binding protein: keeps strands apart
topoisomerase: relieves supercoils ahead of the fork
primase: lays down short RNA primers (shown in yellow)
The end-replication problem and telomeres
When the last primer of the lagging strand is removed there is no
upstream primer to fill the gap, so a linear chromosome shortens.
Telomere: repeat sequence at the end, TTAGGG in humans.
Telomerase: a reverse transcriptase carrying its OWN RNA template,
so it can extend the end with no DNA template.
Most somatic cells have little activity; about 90 percent of cancers restore it.
Origins: one in E. coli, tens of thousands in a human chromosome.
